topic.label: EEG & Signal Methods
topic.description: EEG signal processing, sleep staging, neural time series, modeling, and practical analysis methods.

papers.title: GamSleepNet: A Lightweight Automatic Sleep Staging Framework Based on Gabor Feature Extraction and Mamba Sequence Modeling for Single-Channel EEG.
papers.abstract: Automatic sleep staging is a key technology for the precise diagnosis and treatment of sleep disorders and for long-term home sleep monitoring. Due to its convenience of use, single-channel electroencephalogram (EEG) has become a research focus in home sleep monitoring. However, existing algorithms still face several practical bottlenecks. For example, models with a large number of parameters are prone to overfitting on small labeled datasets; the hardware heterogeneity of customized portable sensors makes datasets not directly shareable; large-scale labeled samples are hard to obtain in real scenarios; there is low recognition accuracy for difficult-to-distinguish sleep stages such as N1 and REM; and there is a lack of suitable research methods for evaluating the required scale of training data for lightweight deployment scenarios. In this paper we propose GamSleepNet, a low-parameter-count automatic sleep staging framework for single-channel EEG. The framework combines a feature extraction module (FEB), which integrates improved Gabor kernels with a learnable filter branch, with a standard Mamba selective state-space model (SSM) used for temporal modeling. A teacher-student feature alignment loss (FAL) and a two-stage training strategy are introduced to enhance the discriminative ability for difficult sleep stages. In addition, following the established paradigm of varying the training dataset's size and observing the performance curve, we make four adaptations tailored to sleep staging, thereby determining the appropriate training data volume for GamSleepNet and providing a methodological reference for determining the training data scale required for deploying other models. Under the limited-labeled-subject setting of the Sleep-EDF dataset, the model has 30.86 k parameters and achieves an overall accuracy of 87.86% and a macro F1 score of 82.62%-the highest values among the compared models-and improves the recognition of difficult REM and N1 samples. The model still maintains stable staging performance under low signal-to-noise ratio and label-scarce scenarios.

ai.topic: Lightweight sleep staging with Gabor features and Mamba SSM
ai.reason: Directly targets CPU-friendly single-channel EEG sleep staging with spectral feature extraction and state-space modeling, matching core interests closely.
ai.summary: Proposed GamSleepNet, a lightweight single-channel EEG sleep-staging framework combining improved Gabor feature extraction with a learnable filter branch and a Mamba selective state-space model, plus teacher-student feature alignment and two-stage training. On Sleep-EDF it reached 87.86% accuracy and 82.62% macro-F1 with only 30.86k parameters, improving recognition of difficult N1 and REM stages and remaining stable under low SNR and label scarcity.

papers.title: A Temporally Causal Two-Layer Framework for Wearable EEG Sleep Staging and Short-Horizon Sleep-Transition Forecasting.
papers.abstract: Reliable online sleep monitoring requires sleep-stage estimates and forecasts based only on information available at the time of prediction. This study developed a temporally causal two-layer framework for wearable electroencephalography (EEG) sleep staging and short-horizon sleep-transition forecasting. Using 128 Bitbrain Open Access Sleep (BOAS) recordings from 100 participants, the first layer (M0) performed five-stage sleep classification with causal signal processing and participant-isolated nested validation. The second layer (M1) used strictly cross-fitted histories of M0 stage probabilities to predict transitions from wake or N1 (W/N1) to N2, N3, or REM sleep (N2+) within 60, 90, or 120 s after each observed 30-s epoch. M1 eligibility was determined from M0-predicted stages during training and evaluation, without requiring polysomnography (PSG) stage labels at inference. M0 achieved 0.830 accuracy and 0.704 macro-F1. Under M0-predicted eligibility, M1 achieved AUROC values of 0.801, 0.791, and 0.786 at 60, 90, and 120 s, respectively; complementary PSG-conditioned evaluation yielded 0.814, 0.803, and 0.801. Prediction was stronger during wakefulness than N1, and the benefits of probability history were specific to the future-sleep task. Future-perturbation tests confirmed unchanged pre-boundary outputs under the tested conditions. A frozen M0 replay on three Muse S Gen2 nights further identified stage-specific limitations in cross-device transfer. These findings establish an auditable framework for temporally causal wearable EEG analysis and demonstrate the potential of short-horizon sleep-transition forecasting while identifying its current generalization boundaries.

ai.topic: Causal wearable EEG sleep staging and transition forecasting
ai.reason: Causal, calibration-aware wearable sleep staging with forecasting is highly transferable to animal sleep and vigilance-state work.
ai.summary: Developed a temporally causal two-layer framework for wearable EEG in which a five-stage sleep classifier (M0) fed cross-fitted stage-probability histories to a second layer (M1) forecasting transitions from wake/N1 to N2/N3/REM within 60-120 s. M0 achieved 0.830 accuracy and 0.704 macro-F1, and M1 reached AUROC 0.801, 0.791, and 0.786 at 60, 90, and 120 s respectively, with cross-device limitations identified on Muse S Gen2 recordings.

papers.title: MG-STNet: A Compact Multi-Granularity Spatiotemporal Network for Adaptive Sleep Staging.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep staging from polysomnography (PSG) is a core component of objective sleep analysis and plays a crucial role in enabling reliable clinical assessment and downstream physiological interpretation, yet the non-stationary nature of physiological signals poses significant challenges for compact models with fixed temporal receptive fields that cannot adapt to time-varying sleep rhythms. To address this challenge, we propose MG-STNet, a compact multi-granularity spatiotemporal network for adaptive sleep staging. The model first utilizes a Multi-Granularity Feature Learning Module (MFLM) to extract multi-resolution representations via parallel downsampling branches, thereby reducing sequence length and computational redundancy. Building on this compact representation, the Global-Local Feature Recalibration (GLFR) module recalibrates multi-channel PSG features by jointly leveraging global statistics and local temporal interactions, while the Adaptive Spatiotemporal Convolution (ASTC) module dynamically routes among complementary temporal branches to capture evolving sleep rhythms. Furthermore, a Temporal Attention Encoding Module (TAEM) is integrated to model long-range dependencies within each epoch. We evaluate MG-STNet on Sleep-EDF-20 and Sleep-EDF-78 using subject-independent k-fold cross-validation. The four-channel model achieves accuracies of 87.3% and 84.5% with 46.6K parameters and 17.2M FLOPs, while its single-channel counterpart achieves 86.6% and 83.2% with 48.6K parameters and 9.8M FLOPs. Experimental results indicate that MG-STNet achieves competitive accuracy with a substantially smaller parameter footprint than mainstream deep sleep-staging models, offering a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for automatic sleep staging under computational constraints.

ai.topic: Compact multi-granularity adaptive sleep staging network
ai.reason: Compact, adaptive spatiotemporal PSG sleep staging aligns strongly with lightweight, generalizable sleep classification interests.
ai.summary: Proposed MG-STNet, a compact multi-granularity spatiotemporal network for sleep staging using parallel downsampling branches, global-local feature recalibration, adaptive spatiotemporal convolution, and temporal attention encoding. On Sleep-EDF-20 and Sleep-EDF-78 it achieved 87.3% and 84.5% accuracy (four-channel, 46.6K parameters) and 86.6% and 83.2% (single-channel), offering a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

papers.title: Operational Definitions of Transition Onset Shape EEG Biomarker Timing in Drowsiness: A Single-Channel Method Comparison.
papers.abstract: Early-warning claims for electroencephalography (EEG)-based drowsiness detection rest on lead times, yet a lead time depends on how onset is operationally defined and is rarely tested against a null. We developed a benchmarking framework and applied it to seven onset estimators and 32 features from single-channel frontal EEG (17 participants, observer-verified drowsiness reports), with external replication in the DROZY dataset (13 sessions with an eligible vigilance-lapse anchor, of 20 retained). Estimator choice shifted onsets by minutes and changed detection coverage from 45% to 100% (Kendall's W = 0.53; external W = 0.71; absolute-agreement intraclass correlation 0.05). In simulation, two-standard-deviation baseline rules flagged onsets in 77-88% of no-change trajectories; null-calibrated thresholds (about 4.6 standard deviations) restored a nominal 5% rate. No estimator showed a statistically detectable excess of onsets in the final 150 s before the anchor relative to spectrum-preserving surrogates, a consensus detector fired before pseudo-anchors as often as before the true anchor, and adding EEG to elapsed session time gave no detectable improvement (area-under-the-curve difference 0.01, 95% confidence interval -0.11 to 0.13). Higuchi fractal dimension and line length correlated weakly with measured electrooculography (|r| ≤ 0.15). We propose interpretability criteria, evidence levels and a reporting checklist for early-onset claims.

ai.topic: Benchmarking onset definitions for EEG drowsiness detection
ai.reason: Rigorous single-channel vigilance-onset benchmarking with null controls is highly relevant to sleep/vigilance state detection methodology.
ai.summary: Built a benchmarking framework to test how operational definitions of transition onset affect EEG drowsiness lead-time claims, applying seven onset estimators and 32 single-channel frontal EEG features across 17 participants with replication in DROZY. Estimator choice shifted onsets by minutes and detection coverage ranged from 45% to 100%, while no estimator showed excess pre-anchor onsets versus surrogate data, prompting proposed interpretability criteria, evidence levels, and a reporting checklist.

papers.title: Neural State Geometry: Unifying Amplitude Landscapes, Coherency Geometry and Information Geometry for EEG State Estimation.
papers.abstract: Brain-state engineering requires measurement and modulation through interpretable, physics-informed coordinates of EEG state structure, change and intervention response. Applications include cognitive fatigue monitoring, neuromodulation readout and progress toward adaptive closed-loop neurotechnology. We introduce Neural State Geometry (NSG), which is a sensor-space framework derived from the complex analytic EEG field rather than a biophysical neuronal model. NSG integrates a Neural Amplitude Landscape (NAL), mapping analytic-amplitude distributions to statistical temperature, internal energy, entropy and heat capacity through exact canonical statistical thermodynamics; pairwise Stokes/coherency geometry representing inter-channel organisation using electromagnetic coherence theory; and quantum-information-inspired state-space geometry quantifying selected-basis organisation. We evaluate NSG through controlled synthetic tests, outcome-blind human-EEG amplitude-model comparison, a single-participant cognitive fatigue example, and a single-investigator transcranial focused ultrasound (TUS) neuromodulation feasibility case. Synthetic tests established descriptor selectivity and common-source sensitivity of zero-lag second-order geometry. NAL/generalised-gamma improved participant-balanced held-out prediction over Rayleigh, Nakagami and gamma but not lognormal. The cognitive fatigue example showed predominantly positive PRE-POST NAL shifts with spectral and second-order deformation. In the fixed-order TUS case, the largest reference-stable NAL displacement occurred at the application site alongside broader sensor-space deformation. NSG provides an interpretable layer for comparing natural and intervention-associated EEG states, supporting future biomarker and target-engagement validation, mechanistic investigation and closed-loop neural engineering.

ai.topic: Neural State Geometry for EEG state estimation
ai.reason: Interpretable, physics-informed state-space and geometry framework for EEG state tracking with strong transfer potential to vigilance-state modeling, though somewhat abstract.
ai.summary: Introduced Neural State Geometry (NSG), a sensor-space EEG framework integrating a Neural Amplitude Landscape mapped to thermodynamic quantities, Stokes/coherency geometry, and quantum-information-inspired state-space geometry, evaluated via synthetic tests, amplitude-model comparison, a cognitive fatigue example, and a transcranial focused ultrasound feasibility case. NSG descriptors showed selectivity in synthetic tests, improved held-out prediction over several amplitude models but not lognormal, and revealed state deformation associated with fatigue and TUS application.

papers.title: Sparse EEG neurodynamics of hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetes with personal euglycemic baseline adaptation.
papers.abstract: Hypoglycemia alters cerebral electrophysiological activity, providing a physiological basis for EEG-based detection. However, translation toward subject-independent monitoring remains constrained by uncertain minimum input requirements, insufficiently characterized stability of sparse representations and their physiological associations, and inter-participant baseline variability. This study benchmarked 24 models spanning engineered-feature machine learning, feature-domain deep learning, and raw-waveform deep learning under leave-one-subject-out validation. Channel-Feature Sparsification was applied using a predefined performance-preservation criterion. Sparse representations were evaluated for selection stability, cross-paradigm concordance, and physiological association. Personal Euglycemic Baseline Adaptation (PEBA) was subsequently applied using a short personal euglycemic reference without participant-specific model retraining. LDA achieved the highest observed balanced accuracy within the engineered-feature paradigm, whereas Sinc-SSNET performed best in both deep-learning paradigms. Sparsification retained the F7 log-theta descriptor for LDA, the F7 channel row for feature-domain Sinc-SSNET, and two channels for raw-waveform Sinc-SSNET. F7 was retained across all three paradigms, and its log-theta descriptor increased during hypoglycemia in 30 of 34 participants (88.2%). PEBA improved balanced accuracy from 0.71 to 0.77 for LDA, from 0.68 to 0.83 for feature-domain Sinc-SSNET, and from 0.71 to 0.78 for raw-waveform Sinc-SSNET. Compared with the corresponding full-input models, reduced configurations decreased parameter counts by 88.51%-99.88%, parameter storage requirements by 87.20%-99.88%, and multiply-accumulate operations by 94.72%-99.91%. These findings demonstrate the preservation of hypoglycemia-related EEG information under a predefined sparsification criterion, while personal euglycemic normalization improves cross-participant discrimination. Physiological consistency and reduced computational requirements support further evaluation of compact EEG-based hypoglycemia detection. Independent cohorts, continuous glycemic-transition recordings, and native sparse EEG acquisition are required before prospective application.

ai.topic: Sparse EEG hypoglycemia detection with personal baseline adaptation
ai.reason: Highly relevant: model benchmarking, channel-feature sparsification, and short per-subject baseline adaptation without retraining map well to calibration and lightweight deployment for sleep/vigilance.
ai.summary: Benchmarked 24 EEG models under leave-one-subject-out validation for hypoglycemia detection in type 1 diabetes and applied Personal Euglycemic Baseline Adaptation (PEBA); PEBA raised balanced accuracy (e.g., 0.68 to 0.83 for feature-domain Sinc-SSNET) while channel/feature sparsification cut parameters by 88.51%-99.88% with the F7 log-theta descriptor increasing during hypoglycemia in 88.2% of participants.

papers.title: Resting-State EEG Features for Distinguishing VS/UWS from MCS: A Comprehensive Univariate Evaluation with Exploratory Multivariate Analysis.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Consciousness assessment in Disorders of Consciousness (DoC) lacks reliable biomarkers. The relative utility of different EEG feature families for distinguishing Vegetative State/Unresponsive Wakefulness Syndrome (VS/UWS) from Minimally Conscious State (MCS) remains unclear. This study systematically compares their discriminative capacity. Methods: Resting-state EEG was recorded from 53 VS/UWSs, 55 MCSs, and 48 healthy controls (HCs). Ten feature families were extracted: spectral power/ratios, Mean Microstate Duration (MMD), Microstate frequency of occurrence (MFO), Microstate coverage (MC), microstate transitions, nonlinear complexity, weighted Phase-Lag Index (wPLI) connectivity, Autocorrelation Window (ACW), and aperiodic 1/f parameters. Features were screened for between-group differences with monotonic trends across VS/UWS, MCS, and HC, correlated with Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R) scores. To obtain unbiased performance estimates and address potential circularity, an exploratory Sparse Group Lasso (SGL) analysis was embedded within a strict nested cross-validation (CV) framework, where all univariate screening, standardization, and hyperparameter tuning were performed exclusively within each outer training fold. Results: Of 101 initial features, 35 wPLI-based metrics were excluded after quality control, leaving 66; of these, 29 showed significant monotonic between-group differences. Partial correlations suggested EEG-CRS-R associations were primarily driven by between-group differences. Microstate transition probabilities showed the strongest univariate discrimination, with the highest AUC for D to A (0.708; sensitivity 60.0%, specificity 77.4%). In the nested CV, the SGL linear predictor achieved a mean outer-fold AUC of 0.632 ± 0.107 (median 0.636) across 37 valid folds, and a nested stable-feature logistic regression yielded a comparable AUC of 0.638 ± 0.099. Notably, family-level selection was highly consistent: Complexity and Microstate Transition families were selected in 74% of outer training folds, followed by MFO (70%) and MMD (70%). Conclusions: Although individual EEG features showed limited discriminative power, and the nested-CV multivariate model did not outperform the best single-feature AUC (0.708), SGL analysis within a nested CV framework identified microstate dynamics and nonlinear complexity as the most robust feature families for distinguishing VS/UWS from MCS. Furthermore, partial correlation analyses indicated that EEG-CRS-R associations were driven by between-group differences, positioning this framework as state-discriminative rather than recovery-monitoring. These findings are exploratory and require further validation in independent external cohorts.

ai.topic: EEG feature families for disorders of consciousness
ai.reason: Systematic comparison of spectral, microstate, complexity, connectivity, ACW, and 1/f features under nested CV; highly transferable interpretable feature-engineering approach for state classification.
ai.summary: Compared ten resting-state EEG feature families across 53 VS/UWS, 55 MCS, and 48 healthy controls, finding microstate transition probabilities the strongest univariate discriminator (D-to-A AUC 0.708) while a Sparse Group Lasso model in nested cross-validation reached only mean AUC 0.632, with microstate dynamics and nonlinear complexity most consistently selected.

papers.title: Participant-Specific Adaptive Label Smoothing Using Subjective Workload Responses for Cognitive Workload Classification from EEG.
papers.abstract: Background: Cognitive workload classification from electroencephalography is affected by interindividual variability in EEG signals and subjective workload responses. We propose participant-specific adaptive label smoothing, in which the change in perceived workload between resting and task conditions controls the target confidence, while the experimental class remains unchanged. Methods: The method was evaluated on the STEW dataset and compared with five alternative supervision strategies. Two classification models were used: a feature-based convolutional neural network and a multi-scale Swin Transformer network (MST-Net) operating on time-frequency representations. Global and participant-specific stratified normalization were evaluated using participant-disjoint cross-validation. The participant-specific approach used normalization statistics estimated from each unseen participant's own unlabeled EEG data. Results: Under stratified normalization, adaptive label smoothing produced the highest macro F1 for both models, with values of 0.768 and 0.796, and ROC AUC values of 0.844 and 0.878, respectively. It also maintained high recall for both classes. Conclusions: The findings suggest that participant-specific subjective workload responses can be used to modulate target confidence, with the most consistent benefit observed under participant-specific normalization. As the strategies differ in target definitions and no hard rest/task or fixed label-smoothing control was evaluated, the differences are descriptive.

ai.topic: Participant-specific adaptive label smoothing for EEG workload
ai.reason: Small-data calibration via participant-specific normalization and label smoothing is directly relevant to user calibration interests.
ai.summary: Proposed participant-specific adaptive label smoothing, where changes in subjective workload between rest and task set target confidence, and evaluated it on the STEW EEG dataset with a feature-based CNN and a multi-scale Swin Transformer under participant-disjoint cross-validation, achieving the highest macro F1 (0.768 and 0.796) and ROC AUC (0.844 and 0.878) under stratified normalization.

papers.title: Incremental Value of EEG Beyond EMG for Participant-Independent Forecasting of Bilateral Lower-Limb Joint Angles.
papers.abstract: Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) may contain gait information without improving forecasts beyond electromyography (EMG). We evaluated this increment in 163 treadmill trials from 57 healthy participants (145,885 prediction origins). Six bilateral lower-limb angles were forecast approximately 124.6 ms ahead on the released grid using two-second EEG band powers and EMG features, ridge regression, and 5 × 4 participant-disjoint nested validation. Shared-penalty fusion produced no false-discovery-rate-significant gain over EMG-only and reduced R2 for the left knee (ΔR2 = -0.0260, q = 0.0072) and left ankle (ΔR2 = -0.0390, q = 0.0222). Its descriptive mean increment was -0.0156 (95% CI -0.0312 to 0.0004). Separate penalties did not establish an advantage (mean ΔR2 = -0.0009, 95% CI -0.0123 to 0.0084). An additional C3/Cz/C4 analysis likewise did not establish mean improvement within its fixed exploratory grid (mean ΔR2 = -0.0006, 95% CI -0.0074 to 0.0058). Extending EEG penalties downward left selected models and predictions unchanged. Current-angle, speed-adjusted, and low-gamma-excluded comparisons revealed no reliable gain; EEG-only did not reliably outperform the training mean. These findings apply to the tested predictors in healthy walking. They do not establish equivalence, identify a neuroanatomical cause, or assess intention decoding in patients with weak, unreliable, or spastic activation.

ai.topic: EEG vs EMG for joint-angle forecasting
ai.reason: Rigorous participant-disjoint validation of EEG/EMG feature fusion with ridge regression; relevant for normalization and cross-subject generalization lessons, though the negative result and kinematics focus limit it.
ai.summary: Tested whether EEG adds predictive value beyond EMG for forecasting six bilateral lower-limb joint angles ~124.6 ms ahead across 163 treadmill trials from 57 participants using participant-disjoint nested validation, and found no significant gain from multimodal fusion, with shared-penalty fusion reducing R2 for left knee and left ankle.

papers.title: Auditable Multiscale EEG Fusion for Offline Cognitive Workload Decoding in COG-BCI.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Provenance checks and target-data access are often poorly documented in cross-participant electroencephalography (EEG) workload studies. An auditable multiscale decoder is evaluated for the 0-back versus 2-back contrast in the public COG-BCI dataset. Methods: Multiscale spectral, covariance, and bilateral features were selected from training data alone. Linear discriminant analysis and support vector machines were then combined. Identical N-back signal files were found under two nominal identifiers during a source audit. One identifier was excluded. Nominal-unit-held-out evaluation covered 23 test units, 10,682 windows, and 138 recordings. Each test unit was excluded from all supervised steps. Unlabeled target data were available for alignment. Results: Mean window balanced accuracy (BA) was 80.70% (SD, 11.23 points; median, 80.39%; range, 55.48-99.36%; descriptive 95% bootstrap interval, 76.15-85.18%). The mean unit area under the curve (AUC) was 0.8770, and pooled recording BA was 86.96%. A re-centered Riemannian minimum-distance-to-mean comparator reached 68.21%. BA fell by 16.39 points without target alignment. No reliable difference was observed for single temporal widths or linear-margin control. Conclusions: The audited pipeline supports offline, transductive decoding within one cohort. Because the cohort informed development, the estimates are internal and post hoc. Independent-cohort validation and evaluation with a fully causal processing pipeline are required.

ai.topic: Auditable multiscale EEG fusion with target alignment
ai.reason: Multiscale spectral features, target-data alignment, and auditable cross-participant validation are useful methodological elements for calibration.
ai.summary: Evaluated an auditable multiscale spectral/covariance EEG decoder for 0-back versus 2-back cognitive workload in the COG-BCI dataset using nominal-unit-held-out validation, reporting mean window balanced accuracy of 80.70% and mean unit AUC of 0.8770, with no reliable advantage for single temporal widths and a 16.39-point BA drop without target alignment.

papers.title: AI-Driven Non-Invasive Scalp EEG Biosensing for Real-Time Seizure Prediction Using Lightweight Gradient Boosting Ensembles.
papers.abstract: Clinical translation of non-invasive scalp electroencephalography (EEG) seizure prediction is severely hindered by patient-dependency, elevated false alarm rates, and excessive computational latency. This study introduces a computationally lightweight, patient-independent machine learning pipeline designed to achieve cross-patient generalization and robust false alarm suppression without requiring subject-specific calibration. Using the continuous multi-channel scalp EEG dataset from the CHB-MIT benchmark (materials/setting), signals underwent dual-stage filtering (1-70 Hz bandpass, 60 Hz notch), artifact removal via Extended FastICA, and Common Average Referencing. Dimensionality was reduced via Principal Component Analysis (12 orthogonal components, >95.4% variance explained). Continuous streams were partitioned into 5 s sliding windows (90% overlap) to extract multi-domain temporal, spectral, and discrete wavelet features, subsequently pruned via ANOVA F-testing to 168 salient predictors. Pre-ictal transitions (20 to 5 min prior to seizure onset, incorporating an excluded 5 min prediction horizon buffer) were classified using a synchronized ensemble of regularized XGBoost and leaf-wise LightGBM models. Dual-model coincidence was governed by a 30 s moving temporal alignment window coupled with 12-epoch persistence smoothing and a 30 min refractory lockout. To prevent intra-subject data leakage, multi-session recordings from the same individual (Cases 01 and 21) were strictly co-located within the training set, and the pipeline was evaluated on an isolated cohort of four completely unseen subjects (Patients 20, 22-24) across 156.5 continuous, unsampled hours. On the independent unseen test cohort, the post-processed framework achieved a primary event-level seizure sensitivity of 100% (34/34 seizures detected; 95% Clopper-Pearson CI: 89.72-100.0%), mathematically bounded by the test sample size, with a false alarm rate of 0.415/h (an 89.5% reduction versus the raw ensemble) and a mean Seizure Prediction Horizon of 17.03 min. Under continuous 0.5 s sliding-window streaming (designed for real-time edge persistence filtering), the framework demonstrated 99.80% operational pre-ictal alert consistency (60,772/60,894 sliding windows; specificity: 98.64%, precision: 91.20%, F1-score: 95.31%). Evaluated on strictly independent, non-overlapping 5 s epochs (N = 6120), the ensemble retained a pre-ictal sensitivity of 99.1%, confirming robust performance independent of window overlap. Execution latency was 0.0057 ms per window, delivering a >1000× speedup over state-of-the-art 3D-CNN and Transformer architectures. By eliminating multi-session data leakage and mitigating clinical alarm fatigue, this pipeline offers reliable cross-patient generalizability, practical intervention timing, and ultra-low computational latency suitable for real-time deployment on low-power wearable closed-loop neurostimulation devices.

ai.topic: Lightweight gradient boosting EEG seizure prediction
ai.reason: Lightweight, patient-independent EEG pipeline with artifact removal and spectral features is methodologically useful though clinically seizure-focused.
ai.summary: Developed a computationally lightweight, patient-independent machine learning pipeline using an ensemble of regularized XGBoost and LightGBM on CHB-MIT scalp EEG, and on four completely unseen subjects achieved 100% event-level seizure sensitivity (34/34) with a false alarm rate of 0.415/h and a mean prediction horizon of 17.03 min at 0.0057 ms per window.

papers.title: When Subject-Level Validation Is Not Enough: Acquisition Format Confounding in a Public Depression Electroencephalography Archive.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Participant-disjoint evaluation prevents electroencephalography (EEG) windows from crossing training and test partitions, but cannot remove cohort-wide technical variables aligned with outcome. We examined this distinction in the public Mumtaz/HUSM depression EEG archive. Methods: After excluding duplicate groups and performing fixed signal quality controlling, 53 participants were retained. Five whole-head relative-power features were evaluated using nested participant-disjoint class-balanced logistic regression with training-fold local scaling and selection. Results: In this exposed cohort, the model achieved mean balanced accuracy of 0.9158 and ROC-AUC of 0.9363; tested graph-recurrent and domain adaptation models were weaker. A subsequent 1000-shuffle nested permutation audit conditional on the selected five-band pipeline gave p=0.000999. Exploratory controls using file size, raw channel count, and normalized byte rates each achieved balanced accuracy of 0.9046, while duration alone achieved 0.6788. Raw European Data Format (EDF) channel configuration nearly determined archive label: 22/26 controls had 22-channel files, compared to only 1/27 depression-labeled participants (Fisher's exact p=6.80×10-10). Conclusions: These metadata expose a label-aligned acquisition/export structure, showing that strong participant-disjoint performance and permutation significance do not establish depression-specific EEG information when acquisition format and archive label are closely aligned. Therefore, public EEG studies should combine participant isolation with early metadata audits, and should require outcome variation within acquisition strata prior to physiological or clinical interpretation.

ai.topic: Acquisition-format confounding audit in public EEG archive
ai.reason: Methodological caution on dataset confounds and validation design is broadly useful for reproducible EEG pipelines.
ai.summary: Audited the public Mumtaz/HUSM depression EEG archive and found that, despite 0.9158 balanced accuracy under nested participant-disjoint validation, acquisition metadata were label-aligned: 22/26 controls had 22-channel EDF files versus only 1/27 depression-labeled participants (Fisher's exact p=6.80×10-10), so participant isolation alone does not establish depression-specific EEG information.

papers.title: Objective-to-Subjective Sleep Discrepancy in Patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Pilot EEG Study.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Sleep disturbance is common in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), but the relationship between subjectively perceived and objectively measured sleep duration remains poorly understood. This pilot study aimed to compare objective and subjective total sleep time (TST) and to explore clinical factors associated with each measure and the difference between them. It also examined the relationship between this difference and nocturnal blood pressure regulation. Materials and Methods: Twenty-two hospitalized patients with RA underwent overnight sleep monitoring using a portable single-channel electroencephalography (EEG) device and provided subjective estimates of TST for the same night in response to a question asked the following morning. Sleep discrepancy was defined as subjective minus EEG-derived TST. Associations with clinical variables were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation analysis with false discovery rate correction. Exploratory regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index were performed. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was available for 20 patients. Results: Subjective TST exceeded EEG-derived TST by a median of 82.75 min (p = 0.0008), and the two measurements were not significantly correlated (ρ = 0.119, p = 0.598). A more positive signed sleep discrepancy was associated with lower serum albumin (ρ = -0.723, q = 0.0020), higher C-reactive protein (CRP) levels (ρ = 0.624, q = 0.0134), glucocorticoid use (q = 0.0462), higher DAS28-CRP (q = 0.0495), and greater functional disability (q = 0.0495). Associations with albumin and CRP persisted in separate exploratory models adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index. Patients with a conventional dipper blood pressure (BP) pattern had a lower signed sleep discrepancy than those with other nocturnal BP patterns (p = 0.0087). Conclusions: In this small exploratory study, subjective sleep duration in patients with RA was generally longer than EEG-derived sleep duration. Furthermore, preliminary associations were observed between sleep discrepancy and inflammatory and clinical characteristics, as well as with nocturnal BP patterns. These findings require confirmation in larger studies, and the clinical significance of sleep discrepancy remains uncertain.

ai.topic: Sleep EEG vs subjective sleep discrepancy in RA
ai.reason: Uses overnight single-channel EEG sleep monitoring which is adjacent to animal sleep work, but it is a small clinical pilot without novel methods.
ai.summary: In a pilot study of 22 hospitalized rheumatoid arthritis patients using portable single-channel EEG, subjective total sleep time exceeded EEG-derived TST by a median of 82.75 min and was uncorrelated with it, with a more positive discrepancy associated with lower albumin, higher CRP, glucocorticoid use, higher DAS28-CRP, and functional disability.

papers.title: Source-reconstructed EEG graph signal processing: Pitfalls and workarounds.
papers.abstract: Graph signal processing (GSP) enables studying brain structure-function coupling by examining how functional signals vary on the structural connectome (SC). While traditionally used with fMRI, GSP applied to electroencephalography (EEG) is gaining interest due to EEG's repertoire of brain activities and higher temporal resolution. To this aim, source activities are reconstructed through electrical source imaging (ESI), summarized into parcellated time series via singular value decomposition (SVD), and analyzed using graph Fourier transform based on SC Laplacian's eigenvectors. This study investigates two methodological biases: SVD polarity ambiguity and ESI spatial leakage. Using simulated epileptic spikes, we validated a method to resolve SVD sign ambiguity and tested it on real interictal epileptogenic discharges. We then quantified the leakage effect on simulation, by comparing graph power spectra between ground truth and its ESI reconstruction, across inverse solutions (exact low-resolution electrical tomography [eLORETA], vs. linear constraint minimal variance) conditions (baseline vs. spike), and connectomes (structural vs. Euclidean distance-based [EC]). We found that uncorrected polarity ambiguity increases high-frequency content, a bias mitigated by the proposed sign control. Conversely, ESI leakage inflates low-frequency content, with stronger effect during spikes, for eLORETA and EC. These results suggest caution in GSP-EEG analyses and inform analytical pipeline selection.

papers.title: TurboRhythmPat and Directed Rhythm Lobish: An Explainable Multi-Selector EEG Model for Recognising Attack and Post-Attack States in Multiple Sclerosis.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Multiple sclerosis (MS) advances through attacks and partial recoveries, yet electroencephalography (EEG) has hardly been used to recognise an attack from the period that follows it, and most EEG models neither test unseen patients nor show which rhythm and electrode pair shaped a decision. Methods: We present an explainable model built around TurboRhythmPat, a feature extractor that codes each 15 s, 19-channel segment as 1805 addressable source-rhythm-target routes in five EEG rhythms. Four iterative feature selectors and their six pairwise intersections form ten selector branches, a self-organised k-nearest-neighbour classifier (tkNN) labels every branch, and iterative majority voting fuses the branch outputs. Directed Rhythm Lobish (DRLobish) decodes the routes behind the selected output into rhythm and electrode-pair statements. We analysed 57 recordings from 19 patients recorded during and after an attack and from 19 healthy controls. Results: Under fully nested leave-one-subject-out validation, in which every data-driven choice was made within the training participants, the attack and post-attack recordings of unseen patients were separated with 65.61% segment-level and 76.32% recording-level accuracy, and patient-level accuracy exceeded chance in 13 of 19 patients (Wilcoxon p = 0.0022). The between-person tasks did not exceed chance (37.92%, 52.51% and 33.17%), and the non-nested estimates (85.71% for attack versus post-attack) were inflated by model selection on the test participants. A permutation-based maxT test over all 1805 routes found no route after family-wise correction (smallest adjusted p = 0.076). Conclusions: Because the attack recording always came first, treatment timing was not documented, no dedicated artefact correction was applied, and the controls were older, the differences are not interpreted as relapse-related changes, and larger prospective cohorts are needed before clinical use.

papers.title: Frequency-embedded sequence learning for multi-class EEG-to-text interface.
papers.abstract: A brain-computer interface (BCI) is an emerging technology for decoding users' intentions, enabling speech decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) signals. This study proposes a multi-class (i.e., 5 words or phrases) EEG-to-Text classification pipeline based on a lightweight 1-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) architecture. The model is trained using both time-domain EEG signals and frequency-embedded power spectral density (PSD) sequences, facilitating systematic comparison of feature representations. EEG signals were preprocessed using a bandpass filter (4 - 120 Hz) and a notch filter (60 Hz) followed by PSD estimation using the modified Welch method. The processed signals were then used to train the proposed 1D-CNN architecture designed for sequential data. In intra-subject evaluation, the proposed approach achieves classification accuracies (mean ± standard deviation) of 46.1 ± 5.1 and 64.4 ± 8.3 using time-domain EEG signals and frequency-embedded PSD sequences, respectively. Peak intra-subject accuracies reach 54% and 82% using EEG signals and PSD sequences, respectively. For inter-subject (pairwise) evaluation, the best observed accuracy is 42%. Inter-subject (pooled) performance remains near chance level (23.3 ± 1.0 and 24.5 ± 0.4), highlighting inter-subject generalization as a key challenge in EEG-based BCI systems. These results demonstrate that while intra-subject performance is promising, inter-subject generalization remains a major limitation. Overall, the proposed approach demonstrates the potential of frequency-embedded PSD representations for improving EEG-based imagined speech classification, while motivating further work toward robust, user-independent BCI systems.

papers.title: A whole-brain neural mass model incorporating astrocyte calcium dynamics for simulating tDCS-induced EEG modulation.
papers.abstract: Understanding the mechanism of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS) requires consideration of important brain cells and their interactions as well as biophysical aspects. Despite recent physiological studies showing sudden calcium signaling associated with astrocyte cells under tDCS, previous computational models aimed at simulating the effects of tDCS, have not included this cell in their equations. This paper proposes a mesoscopic model composed of astrocyte subpopulations as well as pyramidal neurons and interneurons populations. The model can simulate the effect of tDCS on cortical activity related to the average Somatosensory Evoked Potential (aSEP) and is verified by actual results from previous experimental studies on rats. Then a large-scale network model of 76 cerebral areas is considered to simulate the effect of tDCS on EEG signals from 62 scalp electrodes. Actual head meshes and electrodes are used to calculate the distribution of the electric field produced at the cortical level. The model's superiority over previous models lies in its inclusion of astrocyte cells and their interactions with neurons in the neuronal population as well as the simultaneous use of the real human brain connectome to interconnect different cerebral regions. Model parameters are set to produce alpha-like activity in simulated EEG signals. In this study, we focus on the astrocyte-mediated component of tDCS-induced modulation. Results show an increase in the power of the alpha band as well as high frequency components with greater power due to tDCS.

papers.title: Machine Learning Decoding of Dystonic States from EEG-LFP Signals in GPi-DBS: A Multimodal Case Study.
papers.abstract: Programming Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) for pediatric dystonia remains largely empirical, as no validated electrophysiological biomarker currently guides parameter selection, and most studies treat each signal modality separately rather than exploiting their joint structure. In a single pediatric patient with generalized dystonia and bilateral globus pallidus internus (GPi) DBS implantation, we synchronized electroencephalography (EEG), local field potential (LFP), and electromyography (EMG) recordings across seven sessions spanning stimulator-OFF and multiple stimulation intensities. Dystonic muscle activity labels were derived from a validated quantitative EMG pipeline. Regularized logistic regression classifiers, trained on EEG-only, LFP-only, and combined EEG-LFP feature sets, were evaluated under four validation schemes: within-OFF cross-validation, OFF-to-ON generalization, a mixed leave-one-recording-out (LORO) scheme, and generalization to unseen stimulation intensities. The Combined model performed best in the mixed LORO scenario (balanced accuracy 0.74, sensitivity 0.78, specificity 0.70), inheriting a favorable trade-off from the complementary biases of EEG (sensitivity-dominated) and LFP (specificity-dominated). LFP-derived Hjorth mobility, the beta/gamma power ratio, EEG central alpha power, and central-temporal gamma coherence ranked among the most consistent candidate predictive features across scenarios. Generalization to unseen stimulation intensities preserved a similar, moderately degraded performance profile (balanced accuracy 0.66-0.70). These findings provide proof-of-concept evidence that multimodal EEG-LFP decoding can identify epochs of dystonic muscle activity in paediatric dystonia.

The combined EEG-LFP model achieved balanced accuracy 0.74 in mixed leave-one-recording-out validation (sensitivity 0.78, specificity 0.70), with moderately degraded performance (0.66-0.70) on unseen stimulation intensities.

papers.title: Source-Level Multiscale Granger Causality from Preictal Scalp EEG Identifies Candidate Seizure-Onset Zones in Drug-Resistant Focal Epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Precise localization of seizure-onset zones (SOZs) from noninvasive electroencephalography (EEG) remains challenging in the presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant focal epilepsy. We investigated whether cortical source reconstruction combined with multiscale spectral Granger causality (GC) analysis of preictal scalp EEG could identify candidate SOZ regions. Methods: Sixteen participants underwent presurgical evaluation; two were excluded for excessive EEG artifacts, leaving 14 participants (seven resected with Engel class I outcomes and seven unresected). A clinically representative 20 s preictal EEG segment was cleaned using independent component analysis, EEG source solutions were reconstructed with sLORETA on a template head model, and the EEG source activities were then parcellated into 68 Desikan-Killiany cortical regions. Nonparametric GC using Janashia-Lagvilava spectral matrix factorization was estimated in four bands (1-12, 13-30, 30-45, and 55-95 Hz). Regional causal inflow, outflow, and net flow were calculated. Candidate SOZ regions were defined as those exceeding the 95th percentile of absolute net-flow values. Concordance was assessed against clinically determined SOZ localization and, in resected cases, postoperative surgical outcome. Results: Using beta (13-30 Hz) as the primary band, we found that candidate SOZ regions were concordant with clinical localization in 6/7 resected participants (85.7%; exact 95% CI, 42.1-99.6%) and 3/5 scorable prospective participants (60.0%; 14.7-94.7%), yielding 9/12 overall (75.0%; 42.8-94.5%). Two prospective participants lacked sufficient clinical localization for assessment. Three resected participants with left mesial temporal epilepsy showed reproducible left parahippocampal dominance across beta, gamma, and high-gamma bands, with variable entorhinal co-involvement. Top-ranked candidate SOZ regions consistently exhibited net causal inflow. Conclusions: In this small, heterogeneous cohort, source-level net-flow mapping of preictal scalp EEG identified clinically plausible candidate SOZ regions; these exploratory findings suggest a potential noninvasive adjunct to presurgical evaluation. The inflow-dominant pattern supports a receiver-like role of the SOZ. Larger prospective studies with individualized head models, multiple seizures, and intracranial EEG validation will help establish robustness and clinical utility.

Candidate SOZ regions were concordant with clinical localization in 6/7 resected participants and 3/5 scorable prospective participants (9/12 overall), with top-ranked regions showing net causal inflow.

papers.title: EEG Theta Power as an Indicator of Cognitive Workload in Student Pilots.
papers.abstract: Aviation operates within a highly cognitively demanding environment, where assessing pilot workload is essential for preventing errors and accidents associated with excessive or insufficient cognitive demand. This study presents a neurophysiological experiment designed to assess pilot brain activity using electroencephalography (EEG) in a high-fidelity Pilatus PC-21 flight simulator. The study focuses on the theta frequency band (4-8 Hz), given its association with mental effort and cognitive engagement. EEG signals were recorded from eight scalp locations in ten pilots during baseline conditions and three flight simulation modules with different levels of task difficulty. Subjective workload was assessed using the NASA-TLX questionnaire, completed after each simulation phase. The results showed higher theta power during the most cognitively demanding flight phase, particularly across frontal, temporal, and occipital regions. NASA-TLX results similarly indicated increased mental demand, effort, and frustration in the scenario associated with the highest cognitive workload. However, correlation analysis revealed a weak and inconsistent relationship between subjective workload ratings and EEG-derived theta measures across participants, with no clear or statistically significant overall association at the group level. These preliminary results indicate that scalp-recorded theta activity is sensitive to changes in task difficulty during flight simulation. However, given the exploratory nature of the study, the absence of flight-performance metrics, and the lack of strong correlation with subjective ratings, theta-band modulation should be interpreted as an index of task demand rather than a fully consolidated operational workload estimator.

papers.title: MSST-TCN: A Spatially Adaptive Multi-Scale Temporal Convolutional Network for Resting-State EEG-Based Depression Recognition.
papers.abstract: Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) exhibits complex spatial correlations, nonstationarity across multiple scales, and substantial individual differences. Effective extraction of discriminative spatiotemporal features therefore remains a major challenge in automated depression recognition. To address these issues, this study proposes MSST-TCN, a depression recognition model that integrates spatial adaptive filtering with multi-scale temporal modeling. First, the Spatial Adaptive Filtering (SAF) module combines learnable spatial projection, electrode-topology information, and channel recalibration to optimize spatial feature representations of multichannel EEG. The Multi-Scale Dilated Convolution (MSDC) module then extracts dynamic features at different local temporal scales. Finally, the Temporal Attention Pooling (TAP) module combines attention weighting with global average pooling to adaptively aggregate temporal features. The model was evaluated using 53 participants from the MODMA dataset (24 patients with MDD and 29 healthy controls) under a stratified five-fold cross-validation protocol with mutually exclusive training, validation, and test participants. MSST-TCN achieved a mean window-level accuracy of 84.71 ± 2.49% and a participant-level accuracy of 81.13% (43/53; Wilson 95% CI: 68.64-89.41%), improving mean window-level accuracy by 6.41 percentage points over the single-scale TCN baseline. Core-module ablations showed that the complete model outperformed the baseline in all five test folds. In the fine-grained ablation comparisons, some configurations achieved favorable performance point estimates; however, all corresponding participant-paired 95% confidence intervals included zero, and statistically reliable independent performance gains from individual internal components could not be established. Sensitivity analyses further demonstrated relatively consistent classification performance under the examined participant partitioning, window segmentation, and normalization settings. These findings indicate that jointly modeling spatial feature representations, multi-scale local temporal dynamics, and temporal information aggregation can improve EEG-based depression recognition under the current participant-independent evaluation conditions. MSST-TCN thus provides a spatiotemporal feature-learning approach with potential for further application-oriented exploration in EEG-based assisted depression recognition.

papers.title: Age-Adjusted Exploratory Analysis of Spectral, Aperiodic, and Microstate Electroencephalography Features in Multiple Sclerosis.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) can characterize functional brain alterations in multiple sclerosis (MS), but many EEG features vary with age. We, therefore, examined resting-state EEG associations with MS using age-adjusted models while explicitly accounting for the severe age imbalance in the available dataset. Resting-state 128-channel EEG data from the BrainLat dataset were analyzed. Demographic files included 32 patients with MS and 32 healthy controls (HC); global-feature models included 29 patients with MS and 32 HC, and channel-level sample sizes varied by feature. Diagnosis and age were entered in linear models. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied separately to five global spectral/aperiodic tests, 16 global microstate tests, and the 128 channel-wise tests within each feature. Within-MS continuous age regression and exploratory age-stratified ANOVA were evaluated with the same family definitions. After correction, diagnosis coefficients were significant for global bandwidth (β = 1.928, q = 0.0287), global aperiodic offset (β = 1.816, q = 3.29 × 10-7), and offset at all 128 channels (β range = 1.52-2.41; q range = 3.56 × 10-8 to 7.43 × 10-5). Global central frequency, exponent, power spectral density, and all 16 microstate measures did not survive FDR correction. No within-MS continuous-age or age-stratified result survived FDR correction. Aperiodic offset showed the strongest diagnosis association under the specified age-adjusted model. However, the MS and HC age ranges did not overlap (21-55 vs. 56-83 years), so the diagnosis coefficient depends on extrapolation and cannot establish an MS-specific effect. The findings are exploratory and require age-matched replication with detailed clinical, vigilance, site, sex, and magnetic resonance imaging characterization.

papers.title: Physiology-Guided Spiking Neural Networks for EEG Motor-Imagery Recognition.
papers.abstract: Motor-imagery electroencephalography (EEG) decoding depends on rhythm-specific modulation, cue-locked temporal evolution, and structured electrode topology, yet many decoders treat EEG as a generic multichannel time series. (1) Background: A physiological prior that stays in preprocessing cannot constrain what the decoder represents, and spiking networks let such a prior act on the event code itself. (2) Methods: We introduce PG-SNN, which embeds EEG priors in the event code, spatial operator, temporal dynamics, and readout. A causal eventizer converts EEG into sparse, sign-preserving spikes using rhythm-sensitive, temporal-change, and montage-contrast operators; an electrode-prior graph restricts message passing to local montage adjacency and homologous inter-hemispheric coupling; and a multi-timescale adaptive spiking backbone represents rapid event transitions and slower mu/beta modulation. (3) Results: On BCI Competition IV-2a the model reaches 84.72% accuracy (kappa = 0.796), 2.56 and 5.64 percentage points above the strongest matched ANN and SNN baselines; on the EEGMMIDB four-class subject-independent protocol, it reaches 71.28% (kappa = 0.617), 3.86 points above the strongest matched ANN baseline, and a fifteen-variant ablation attributes the largest single effect to the event code. (4) Conclusions: Embedding sensorimotor physiology into event generation, spatial propagation, and spike dynamics is a practical route to compact motor-imagery decoders, within the limits of the two benchmarks and the single shared protocol.

papers.title: Exploratory Assessment of Portable EEG- and PPG-Derived Indices Following High-Intensity Exercise Under Partial Sleep Restriction in Young Men.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: This exploratory study investigated associations between partial sleep restriction and portable device-derived prefrontal EEG and PPG indices, heart rate recovery (HRR), and perceived exertion (RPE) after high-intensity exercise in young men. Methods: Forty healthy men were randomly assigned to a normal sleep group (NSG; ~8 h, n = 20) or a sleep-restricted group (SRG; ~4 h, n = 20). Participants performed the Harvard Step Test (HST). Prefrontal EEG (Fp1 and Fp2) and single-site PPG were recorded for 1 min before and immediately after exercise using a portable consumer-grade device. Heart rate (HR), HRR, RPE, and physical fitness were assessed. Data were analyzed using mixed-design analysis of variance, t-tests, and supplementary linear mixed-effects models with Holm correction. Results: The theta-to-beta ratio (TBR) showed a significant group × time interaction (Holm-adjusted p = 0.034), increasing only in the SRG (p = 0.0014), whereas spectral edge frequency at 90% (SEF-90) showed no interaction (p = 0.781). Significant interactions were observed for the heart rate variability (HRV) index (p = 0.0085), sympathetic-related index (p < 0.001), and parasympathetic-related index (p = 0.0063). The HRV index decreased and the sympathetic-related index increased only in the SRG, whereas the parasympathetic-related index decreased in both groups. During recovery (1-3 min), the SRG had higher HR and lower HRR than the NSG (all p < 0.05). RPE was also higher in the SRG (p = 0.013). All reported p-values were Holm-adjusted. Conclusions: Partial sleep restriction was associated with changes in prefrontal EEG and exploratory PPG-derived indices, lower early HRR, and greater perceived exertion. The selective TBR response suggests index-dependent EEG changes. These findings warrant caution because of limited EEG spatial coverage, brief recordings, potential artifacts, and unvalidated proprietary algorithms. Device-derived changes do not directly establish altered central or autonomic neural activity.

papers.title: EEG Functional Connectivity for Consumer Preference Prediction: Statistical Network Analysis and Stable Connectivity Signatures.
papers.abstract: Background: Electroencephalography (EEG) is increasingly used to investigate consumer preferences; however, most predictive studies rely on local spectral or temporal features, and the predictive and statistical relevance of functional connectivity remains underexplored. This study evaluated the statistical significance, predictive performance, and feature-selection stability of EEG functional connectivity measures associated with consumer preference. Methods: Phase Locking Value (PLV) and Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) were computed for the delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma frequency bands using product-related EEG recordings from the NeuMa dataset. Subject-level paired statistical analyses were performed with false discovery rate correction. PLV, NMI, and early feature-level PLV+NMI fusion were evaluated using LASSO-based feature selection and five machine-learning classifiers under stratified 10-fold and subject-independent leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) validation. Feature-selection stability was assessed under both validation strategies. Results: Preferred-product viewing was associated with widespread reductions in functional connectivity for both PLV and NMI, with NMI showing particularly extensive differences in the delta band. PLV and NMI yielded broadly comparable predictive performance, with the highest balanced accuracy of 0.699 achieved by PLV combined with Naive Bayes under both stratified 10-fold and LOSO validation. Early PLV+NMI fusion did not improve predictive performance. In contrast, NMI-derived features dominated the fused stability ranking, accounting for 18 of the 20 highest-ranked stable features, predominantly in the delta band. Conclusions: EEG functional connectivity provides complementary information about consumer preference at the statistical, predictive, and feature-stability levels. PLV combined with Naive Bayes provided the highest balanced accuracy, whereas NMI exhibited greater statistical sensitivity and feature-selection stability. These findings highlight low-frequency, particularly delta-band, connectivity as a relevant target for further investigation and demonstrate the importance of evaluating EEG representations beyond classification performance alone.

papers.title: Development and Evaluation of a Cap-Mounted Tripolar Concentric Ring Electrode System with a Central Gel-Delivery Opening for tEEG and EEG Recording.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) commonly uses conventional disc electrodes with conductive gel or paste to record electrical activity from the scalp. However, conventional disc electrodes have limited spatial selectivity because they detect electrical activity spreading from different brain regions. Tripolar concentric ring electrodes (TCREs) have been developed to improve spatial selectivity by estimating the scalp surface Laplacian. Nevertheless, establishing electrical contact at hair-bearing scalp locations remains challenging. To address this challenge, we developed a modified gold-plated copper TCRE with a 2 mm central opening for conductive gel delivery and a custom 3D-printed cap-mounted holder. After electrode placement, conductive gel is delivered through the opening to establish electrical contact between the metallic contacts and the scalp beneath the hair. The system was evaluated in ten healthy adults using eyes-open/eyes-closed resting-state EEG and pattern-reversal checkerboard visual stimulation. For the experimental recordings, two modified TCREs were positioned at the occipital scalp locations O1 and O2, where conductive gel was delivered through their central openings to establish electrical contact with the scalp. A third TCRE was positioned at Pz and coupled using conductive paste, while a separate conventional disc electrode was placed 1 cm superior to Pz. Recordings from these electrode configurations were analyzed to evaluate resting-state alpha activity, visual evoked potentials (VEPs), and signal quality. Each TCRE provided tripolar EEG (tEEG) and EEG Emulator (eEEG) signals. The modified TCREs recorded identifiable VEP components, with negative and positive peaks near 105 and 141 ms, respectively, along with stimulus-related spectral activity. The eEEG VEP waveforms at O1 and O2 showed strong correlations with Pz eEEG (median r=0.897 and 0.938, respectively). Alpha-band power also increased significantly during eye closure in both gel-coupled tEEG channels (Holm-adjusted p=0.0195). Impedance measurements, signal-quality analyses, and circuit modeling provided additional characterization of the system. These findings support the feasibility of acquiring tEEG and eEEG signals using the modified TCRE system at hair-bearing scalp locations.

papers.title: Decision-Aligned Value Learning for Selective Adoption of EEG Fusion in Human-Robot Collaboration
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) captures neural activity associated with human perception and decision-making. It provides human-robot collaboration (HRC) systems with measurable evidence for event recognition, situation assessment, and action preparation. External sensing cannot easily provide such evidence. However, the quality and complementarity of this evidence vary across samples, and existing EEG fusion methods do not explicitly determine when EEG improves a prediction. We therefore framed selective EEG use as a sample-wise incremental-value estimation problem and proposed Value Estimation and Constraint-Aware Triage for Adoption (VECTA). VECTA separates the generation of an EEG-informed Fusion prediction from the decision about whether it should replace the existing Base prediction. The framework uses system gain to quantify the loss reduction from Base to Fusion and matching gain to assess whether benefits arise from sample-matched EEG. A signed-value learner estimates system gain from decision-time evidence and prioritizes high-value Fusion outputs under budget constraints. Cross-subject evaluations on three HRC datasets showed that matched Fusion outperformed shuffled controls. Estimated gains tracked realized gains, with Spearman correlations of 0.347-0.612 and positive-gain areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) of 0.708-0.842. Under budget constraints, VECTA reduced Brier loss and harmful Fusion adoption and achieved the highest mean normalized AUBC across three datasets among the selective-decision methods evaluated. Validation on three external multi-modal datasets showed that VECTA could be applied directly as a post-hoc decision layer to task-specific predictors without retraining. These results show that selective Fusion adoption can translate the uneven utility of EEG into system-level gains.

papers.title: Quantitative EEG Differences Across Two Sedation Conditions in a Child with Epilepsy: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Sedation is frequently required to obtain electroencephalography (EEG) recordings in children with neurodevelopmental disorders and structural etiologies of epilepsy. However, the extent to which different sedative agents influence quantitative interictal epileptiform discharge (IED) burden remains insufficiently characterized. A child with congenital cytomegalovirus-associated structural brain injury underwent EEG recordings under two sedation conditions: continuous low-dose propofol infusion and oral chloral hydrate. Quantitative analyses were performed using a duration-matched, within-subject design. Artifact-minimized EEG segments of equal duration (15.52 min) were analyzed. IED burden was quantified using spike frequency (spikes/min) and spike index (percentage of 10 s epochs containing ≥1 spike). Spectral power distribution and spectral edge frequency (SEF95) were also evaluated. The chloral hydrate recording showed a higher observed spike frequency than the propofol recording (14.11 vs. 4.12 spikes/min; descriptive rate ratio, 3.42) and a higher 10-s spike index (84.95% vs. 27.96%). Spectral analysis demonstrated lower SEF95 and greater delta predominance in the propofol recording, whereas the chloral hydrate recording showed relatively greater theta-alpha activity. The two recordings showed marked differences in apparent IED burden and background spectral characteristics. However, because they were obtained approximately one year apart and under different clinical circumstances, including intercurrent illness during the chloral hydrate recording, these differences cannot be attributed specifically to the sedative agents. This case illustrates the importance of considering sedation, clinical context, and vigilance state when longitudinally interpreting quantitative pediatric EEG findings.

papers.title: PHQ-9-Guided Ordinal Contrastive Learning for Severity-Aware EEG Depression Representation Learning.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based depression detection studies commonly reduce clinical severity scores, such as the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), to binary diagnostic labels, thereby discarding ordinal information that may be useful for representation learning. This study proposes PHQ-9-guided ordinal contrastive learning (CE+OC), a training objective that uses PHQ-9 scores as privileged ordinal supervision during training while requiring only EEG at inference. PHQ-9 severity distances guide contrastive pair selection and scale the embedding separation margin, using clinical distances to guide the latent EEG space without an explicit patient-ranking objective. The method was evaluated on the Multi-modal Open Dataset for Mental-Disorder Analysis (MODMA) using strict leave-one-subject-out cross-validation across 53 subjects with 128-channel resting-state EEG. The primary representation finding was improved full-cohort PHQ-9 recoverability: a cross-validated held-out PHQ-9 probe showed that CE+OC increased recoverable PHQ-9 rank correlation from 7.8% to 33.6% (paired two-sided permutation p=0.031), an absolute gain of 25.7 percentage points, and reduced mean absolute PHQ-9 error from 27.8% to 22.8% of the 27-point PHQ-9 range (18.1% relative reduction; paired two-sided Wilcoxon p=0.011; bootstrap 95% CI for Δρ: 3.0% to 49.6%). CE+OC also showed descriptive diagnostic differences on MODMA: AUC increased from 59.8% to 69.3%, balanced accuracy from 59.5% to 66.0%, specificity from 69.0% to 86.2%, precision for major depressive disorder (MDD) from 57.1% to 73.3%, and MDD-F1 from 53.3% to 56.4%. False positives decreased from 31.0% to 13.8% of healthy subjects, although sensitivity decreased from 50.0% to 45.8%. A separate LOSO diagnosis evaluation on the independently acquired Mumtaz cohort achieved an AUC of 85.1%; it provides secondary evidence that the pipeline is feasible in a second cohort, but it is not a cross-dataset transfer experiment. A true-diagnosis-only control achieved ρ=0.502 and MAE 2.142 points, and within-MDD probe correlation remained negative (ρ=-0.424). The findings support increased full-cohort PHQ-9 recoverability relative to CE-only, not established information beyond diagnosis; diagnostic difference intervals include zero, and the model is not validated for stand-alone screening.

papers.title: Multidimensional Electrophysiological Responses to TMS on the Primary Motor Cortex: A TMS-EEG Characterization of Immediate Cortical Responses.
papers.abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) combined with electroencephalography (EEG) enables millisecond-scale characterization of cortical responses, but direct multidimensional comparisons across stimulation protocols remain limited. In a randomized within-subject crossover study, 17 healthy adults received 10 Hz repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), 1 Hz rTMS, and intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) over the left primary motor cortex in separate sessions. TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs), power spectral density (PSD), and EEG microstate dynamics were assessed before and immediately after stimulation. Following 10 Hz rTMS, group-level P30 amplitude increased from 0.17 to 0.89 μV, while N45 became less negative from -1.73 to -0.82 μV; PSD increased significantly across 15.5-45 Hz. In contrast, 1 Hz rTMS reduced P30 from 0.68 to 0.39 μV and increased P60 from 0.31 to 1.65 μV, with significant PSD reductions at 12.7-31.7 Hz and 32.2-45 Hz. iTBS reduced the magnitude of N45 from -2.76 to -1.93 μV and decreased P60 from 1.41 to 0.47 μV. These findings demonstrate protocol-specific multidimensional electrophysiological profiles across temporal and spectral measures. This framework facilitates systematic comparison across stimulation protocols and provides a basis for further investigation of TMS-induced cortical responses and individualized neuromodulation.

papers.title: Is Swimming Training Experience Associated with Better Sensorimotor Control in Water? An Exploratory Study of Upper-Limb Joint Position Sense, EEG Activity, and Subjective Workload.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: This study examined whether swimming experience is associated with better sensorimotor control in water by comparing joint position sense, cortical activity, and subjective workload across training backgrounds and environments. Methods: Thirty-six participants (12 swimmers, 12 Chinese Wushu (Wushu) athletes, and 12 untrained individuals) performed continuous shoulder and elbow joint-position-reproduction tasks on land and in water. Joint-angle errors, resting-state and task-related α- and β-band EEG power, and NASA Task Load Index scores were assessed using cluster-based permutation tests and mixed analyses of variance with multiple-comparison correction. Results: Environment affected left-elbow absolute error (p = 0.0015) and constant error at all four joints (all corrected p ≤ 0.0028), without a swimming-specific accuracy advantage. Wushu athletes had lower signed left-shoulder and left-elbow constant errors than swimmers. Swimmers showed a greater water-land increase in resting-state α power than untrained participants before right-side tasks (Holm-adjusted p = 0.0048). Task-related α desynchronization was weaker in water during left-shoulder and left-elbow tasks; no corrected training-related effects emerged for task-related α or β power. Physical demand and perceived performance showed group × environment interactions (both corrected p = 0.0458); swimmers reported lower physical demand than untrained participants in water. Conclusions: Swimming experience was associated with distinct pre-task resting-state α responses, but not better joint-position accuracy or distinct task-related cortical activity modulation. Long-term training in different environments appeared to reduce the physical demand of sensorimotor tasks performed in the familiar environment. These findings provide limited support for swimming-specific sensorimotor advantages in water.

papers.title: EEG Emotion Recognition Based on Azimuthal Equidistant Projection and a Multiscale Residual Temporal Network.
papers.abstract: Background: In most existing EEG-based emotion recognition studies, the spatial configuration of electroencephalography (EEG) electrodes is not adequately preserved, and conventional single-scale convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have limited ability to capture both local and global spatial patterns. To address these limitations, an EEG emotion recognition framework integrating azimuthal equidistant projection (AEP) with a multiscale residual temporal network (MRTNet) is proposed. Methods: Differential entropy (DE) features are first extracted, and the three-dimensional electrode coordinates are projected onto a two-dimensional plane to construct AEP-based DE (AEP-DE) feature maps that preserve the spatial topology of the electrode layout. MRTNet then combines multiscale depthwise separable convolutions with a long short-term memory (LSTM) network to extract spatial features at multiple receptive-field scales and model temporal dependencies across EEG segments. Results: Experimental results show that MRTNet achieves average accuracies of 95.1% for four-class classification on the Database for Emotion Analysis using Physiological Signals (DEAP) and 93.1% for three-class classification on the SJTU Emotion EEG Dataset (SEED). Conclusions: Grad-CAM visualizations further indicate that the model responses are concentrated in spatially localized frontal and temporal regions, providing qualitative support for the spatial interpretability of the proposed method.

papers.title: Neural dynamics of resting-state EEG microstates in youth major depressive disorder with suicidal ideation.
papers.abstract: Youth major depressive disorder (MDD) is a debilitating condition associated with high rates of suicidal behavior. Although abnormal neuroimaging alterations have been reported in MDD patients with suicidal ideation (SI), little is known about the mechanisms of brain dynamics at high temporal resolution. This cross-sectional study included 177 participants aged 15-30 years: 95 with drug-naïve MDD (53 with SI, 42 without SI) and 82 healthy controls. All participants underwent a standardized 5-minute resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) acquisition. Comprehensive clinical assessments were administered, including the collection of psychosocial data and evaluation of suicide risk using the Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation (BSI-C). Group differences in microstate parameters were analyzed, and correlations between these parameters and clinical variables were examined. Resting-state EEG microstate analysis indicated that the SI group, relative to the NSI group, exhibited higher occurrence, coverage, and duration of microstate A, along with decreased indices for microstate B and reduced occurrence (but not coverage or duration) of microstate D. Alterations in transition probabilities were most prominent in microstates A and B, highlighting specific network-level differences associated with SI. In the SI group, BSI-C scores were positively correlated with the transition probability from C to B. Our findings suggest that young individuals with MDD and SI show specific changes in microstates, especially A and B. These findings reveal altered EEG microstate dynamics associated with SI in young MDD patients and may inform future research on neurophysiological correlates of suicidal ideation.

papers.title: Hybrid EEG-EOG Brain-Computer Interface for Virtual-Reality Powered Mobility Training in Children with Severe Neuromotor Disabilities: A Multiple-Case Feasibility Study.
papers.abstract: Background: Developing Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) for children with severe neuromotor disabilities remains challenging due to developmental neurophysiology and the high cognitive demands of motor imagery. Hybrid BCIs integrating electroencephalography (EEG) and electrooculography (EOG) can overcome these limitations by combining continuous motor-related control with reliable discrete commands. This multiple-case study investigated the feasibility of a hybrid EEG-EOG BCI integrated with a virtual reality (VR) powered wheelchair simulator for mobility training. Methods: Six participants (mean age: 13.00 ± 3.52 years; 1 female, 5 males) with severe neuromotor disabilities (i.e., Central Core Myopathy, LAMA2 related Congenital Muscular Dystrophy, Spinal Muscular Atrophy Type II, and Cerebral Palsy) completed repeated sessions using a self-paced BCI. The system combined continuous kinesthetic motor imagery (KMI) for steering and EOG-detected voluntary blinks for discrete commands. We evaluated online classification performance (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity), user workload (NASA-TLX), and simulator-related discomfort (MSAQ) under fully and semi-immersive VR conditions. Results: Across the selected session-level evaluations, mean online classification accuracy was 67%, increasing to 77% when considering only successful evaluations. Four of the six participants completed the experimental protocol, whereas two discontinued after T3 because sufficiently stable BCI control could not be achieved. NASA-TLX scores indicated increasing perceived workload but generally low frustration, while low MSAQ scores suggested good VR tolerability. No participants withdrew because of VR-related discomfort or adverse effects. Conclusions: This exploratory study provides preliminary evidence supporting the feasibility of hybrid EEG-EOG BCI control within a VR-based powered mobility simulator for children and adolescents with severe neuromotor disabilities. Although simulated navigation was feasible for four participants, substantial variability in BCI control highlights the need for further technological refinement and validation in larger cohorts.
