papers.title: From hemodynamics to function: the role of fNIRS and hybrid EEG-fNIRS systems in next-generation assistive technologies for rehabilitation.
papers.abstract: Assistive technologies (AT) serve as fundamental tools for rehabilitation because they help people with neurological or physical disabilities to restore their abilities, independence and their overall life satisfaction. Existing AT control methods, which include manual operation, eye tracking, voice commands, electromyography (EMG) and electroencephalography (EEG), have improved rehabilitation results but still face challenges because of their inability to maintain reliable performance during user exhaustion and difficulties operating in challenging situations. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) has recently become a new neuroimaging technique that provides excellent imaging capability, can be used while moving, and has portable design features. fNIRS-based devices such as wheelchairs, robotic prostheses, and brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have proven their ability to decode user intention and assist rehabilitation. The limited ability of fNIRS to measure time intervals prevents its use in real-time systems. The hybrid EEG-fNIRS systems combine EEG technology, which provides high-speed temporal measurements, with fNIRS technology, which provides spatial and hemodynamic measurements. The multimodal techniques combine different measurement methods, which improve accuracy while decreasing false positive results and increasing system adaptability. This review critically examines how AT control modalities have been evolving, and it also measures what fNIRS can do technically, plus what it struggles with, and then it pulls together the available evidence on hybrid EEG-fNIRS systems as a possible way toward more adaptive, user-centered rehabilitation technologies.

papers.title: Differential Neurophysiological Signatures of Asymptomatic Carotid and Intracranial Atherosclerotic Stenosis: A Multimodal Resting-State EEG Study.
papers.abstract: Chronic cerebral hypoperfusion associated with asymptomatic atherosclerotic cerebrovascular stenosis may induce functional-network alterations before overt neurological deficits emerge. Asymptomatic carotid stenosis (ACS) and asymptomatic intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis (aICAS) represent distinct large-artery phenotypes with differing perfusion distributions. However, whether these location-specific hemodynamic constraints are associated with different patterns of functional brain reorganization is poorly understood. This study investigated the multiscale electrophysiological alterations associated with ACS and aICAS. In this cross-sectional study, 68 participants, including ACS (n = 29), aICAS (n = 17), and age-matched healthy controls (n = 22), underwent resting-state electroencephalography (rs-EEG) recording and neuropsychological assessment (Chinese Mini-Mental Status [CMMS], Trail Making Test Parts A and B [TMT-A/B]). Microstate dynamics, power spectra, and α-band source-space functional connectivity were analyzed. Network-Based Statistic (NBS) controlled for family-wise error in connectivity analysis. Partial correlations adjusted for age, hypertension, and diabetes. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) performance was evaluated using bootstrap confidence intervals and repeated five-fold cross-validation. CMMS scores did not differ among groups, whereas TMT completion times were longer in the ACS group, indicating subtle performance alterations. Both patient groups showed reduced microstate A (MsA) coverage and decreased transitions between MsA and microstate C (MsC). ACS additionally exhibited shortened MsA duration, reduced α-band power, and increased connectivity within a distributed network identified by NBS. The aICAS group showed increased bidirectional transitions between microstate B (MsB) and microstate D (MsD) but no significant NBS component. Selected microstate measures remained associated with TMT performance after covariate adjustment. ROC analyses showed moderate discrimination, with apparent areas under the curves (AUCs) of 0.672-0.744 and cross-validated AUCs of 0.675-0.744. ACS and aICAS showed shared and location-specific electrophysiological alterations. These exploratory findings may help characterize early functional brain changes associated with asymptomatic cerebrovascular stenosis, but require confirmation in larger independent cohorts.

Selected microstate measures remained associated with Trail Making Test performance and yielded moderate cross-validated ROC discrimination (AUC 0.675–0.744).

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Auditory Electrophysiological Biomarkers in Alzheimer's Disease and Hearing Loss: A Critical Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with a long preclinical phase, making early biomarker discovery essential for timely diagnosis, risk stratification, and intervention. Hearing loss has increasingly been recognized as a clinically important and potentially modifiable factor associated with cognitive decline and dementia risk. Beyond peripheral auditory impairment, accumulating evidence suggests that central auditory dysfunction, altered auditory processing, and electrophysiological abnormalities may emerge during the course of AD and related cognitive disorders. Auditory electrophysiological signals, including electroencephalography (EEG), auditory event-related potentials (ERP), auditory evoked cortical potentials (AECP), auditory brainstem response (ABR) recordings, cochlear microphonics (CM), and distortion product otoacoustic emission (DPOAE) measures, provide objective and repeatable measurements of peripheral and central auditory pathway function. However, conventional analysis based on peak latency, amplitude, spectral power, and manually engineered features may not fully capture subtle disease-related alterations distributed across time, frequency, and waveform morphology. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers new opportunities to extract high-dimensional and physiologically informative representations from auditory and neural signals. Machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), self-supervised learning (SSL), explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and multimodal modeling can support data-driven biomarker discovery, especially in settings where labeled datasets are limited and electrophysiological changes are subtle. This critical narrative review synthesizes current knowledge at the intersection of hearing loss, AD, auditory electrophysiology, and AI. We discuss traditional signal processing, supervised ML, deep neural networks, self-supervised representation learning, explainable models, and multimodal integration strategies. We also identify major methodological limitations, including small sample sizes, heterogeneous acquisition protocols, insufficient external validation, limited interpretability, data leakage risks, and challenges in translating animal-model findings to human disease. Finally, we propose future directions for trustworthy, interpretable, and multimodal AI systems capable of advancing auditory electrophysiological biomarkers for AD and hearing-related neurodegeneration.

It also identifies methodological limitations including small samples, heterogeneous acquisition, limited external validation and interpretability, and data leakage risks, and proposes directions for trustworthy multimodal AI biomarker systems.

papers.title: Long-Term Music Training Is Associated with Auditory-Frontal Cortical Responses in Mandarin-Speaking Children with Cochlear Implants: A Clinical High-Density EEG Study.
papers.abstract: Background: Children with cochlear implants (CIs) develop speech and language under electrically mediated auditory input, yet it remains unclear whether cumulative musical experience is associated with cortical speech processing. This study examined whether music-training duration was related to prefrontal responses during Mandarin speech-feature processing in children with CIs using high-density electroencephalography (EEG) source localization. Methods: Thirty Mandarin-speaking children with CIs from the Tianjin Little Dolphin Hearing-Loss Children's Choir were grouped by cumulative music-training duration: short (<3 years), medium (3-5 years), and long (>5 years). Participants completed audiological and speech-perception assessments and underwent high-density EEG during a Mandarin multi-feature oddball paradigm including tone, consonant, vowel, duration, and intensity deviants. Mismatch negativity (MMN) responses were source-localized to characterize cortical activation. Results: Behavioral measures, including aided hearing thresholds and speech-perception accuracy, were comparable across groups. In contrast, source analysis showed progressively stronger prefrontal activation with longer music-training duration. This pattern was most evident for vowel and consonant deviants, whereas duration-related responses showed little variation. In adjusted linear models, longer training duration was positively associated with prefrontal activation for intensity (p = 0.002) and tone (p = 0.022), with marginal associations for consonant (p = 0.057) and vowel (p = 0.058) deviants. Conclusions: Longer music-training duration was associated with stronger auditory-frontal cortical responses during Mandarin speech-feature processing in children with CIs, despite comparable behavioral auditory outcomes across groups. These preliminary findings suggest that high-density EEG may provide a complementary clinical neurophysiological tool for evaluating rehabilitation-related cortical differences in pediatric CI users. Future longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether these associations reflect training-related developmental changes.

papers.title: Detecting cognitive motor dissociation in unresponsive brain-injured patients: a prospective cohort study using active task-based EEG.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to assess the prevalence and prognostic value of cognitive motor dissociation (CMD) detected by active task-based electroencephalography (EEG) in a cohort of patients with disorders of consciousness (DoC). In a prospective cohort study, we enrolled 56 consecutive clinically unresponsive patients with acute or chronic brain injury. Patients underwent EEG recording during an active motor imagery task following spoken commands. Functional outcomes were assessed using the Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended (GOS-E) at 6 months. Ten healthy volunteers served as a control group. Among the 56 unresponsive patients, 6 (10.7%) were identified as CMD-positive. The favorable-outcome rate (GOS‑E ≥ 4) was higher in the CMD-positive group (2/6, 33.3%) than in the CMD-negative group (4/50, 8.0%), although the difference did not reach statistical significance (Fisher's exact p = 0.12). At 6‑month follow‑up, no deaths occurred in the CMD‑positive group (n = 6), compared with a mortality rate of 16% (8/50) in the CMD‑negative group. Given the limited sample size, these descriptive results are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger prospective cohorts. In the healthy control group, 9 of 10 participants (90%) were task‑positive; the only task‑negative participant reported having fallen asleep during the experiment. Most healthy volunteers reported feeling drowsy and easily distracted while performing the task. Active task‑based EEG can detect CMD in a subset of behaviorally unresponsive patients, and its presence was descriptively associated with more favorable outcomes. However, the detection rate in our cohort was lower than previously reported, and healthy controls frequently experienced sleepiness during the task. These findings support the prognostic value of EEG‑detected CMD while highlighting the need for more sensitive, patient‑adapted paradigms.

papers.title: Changes in Clinical Management Related to Continuous Versus Routine Electroencephalogram in Critically Ill Adults: Analysis of a Randomized Trial.
papers.abstract: Continuous electroencephalogram (cEEG) is increasingly utilized in the intensive care unit for consciousness-impaired patients with various conditions. It is, however, costly in terms of technical and human resources, and its impact on prognosis compared with routine EEG (rEEG) remains debated. We aimed to characterize the effect of cEEG vs. rEEG on clinical management modifications, and to determine if these correlated with a better outcome. This is an ancillary analysis using data of CERTA (NCT03129438), a randomized trial comparing cEEG versus repeated rEEG in critically ill adults with altered consciousness. Clinical management modifications due to the EEG intervention, predefined as performed within 60 h of EEG start, were prospectively recorded (anti-seizure medication [ASM], sedation, new radiological examination, new surgical intervention, withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy). Correlation with the EEG type was analyzed by 2 × 2 tables; Mantel-Haenszel tests explored the impact on mortality and functional outcome at 6 months. The trial included 364 patients completing follow-up (182 each in the cEEG and rEEG groups). While 58.2% of cEEG and 45.6% of rEEG patients had any management change (p = 0.018), ASM was modified in 22.0% (cEEG) and 12.1% (rEEG) (p = 0.012); other clinical interventions were comparable across EEG groups. Adjusting for ASM modifications, mortality (p = 0.845) and functional outcome (p = 0.619) remained similar between the EEG groups. In critically ill adults, cEEG is associated with more clinical management modifications compared to repeated rEEG, particularly regarding ASM, but this does not seem to translate into improved patients' outcomes.

After adjusting for ASM modifications, 6-month mortality and functional outcome remained similar between EEG groups, indicating that increased management changes did not translate into improved outcomes.
